lead: Valencia celebrates popular and religious festivals all year round, where ritual and ingenuity, gunpowder, flowers, music and purifying fire all mix together.

The extrovert, lively character of Valencians shows in a unique festive calendar: religious and secular festivals held mostly out in the street, where rituals, creativity, gunpowder, music and flowers combine. Three of its traditions have earned UNESCO recognition as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
All the festivals you will find here are free to attend. They are part of the city’s identity and open to anyone who wants to experience them.

items.title: Saint Anthony the Abbot and the Three Kings Parade
items.body: The Valencian Christmas cycle closes with the Three Kings Parade on 5 January, one of the oldest and most moving in Spain, followed by the feast of Saint Anthony the Abbot on 17 January, when domestic animals are blessed at the doors of churches in a ritual that has stayed alive for centuries in several districts of Valencia.
facts: 5 January in the afternoon: the Three Kings parade through the streets of the centre
17 January at churches in the city’s traditional districts

items.title: Saint Vincent the Martyr
items.body: Saint Vincent the Martyr is the patron saint of Valencia and his feast day, 22 January, is celebrated with a solemn Mass in the Cathedral and a procession through the historic centre. The Valencian deacon Vincent was martyred in the 4th century, in the year 304. The Crypt of the San Vicente Prison, beneath the Town Hall, shows the remains of the place where, according to tradition, he was held prisoner.
facts: 22 January: a celebration attended by civil and religious authorities
A route along the historic streets with the image of the martyr

items.title: Las Fallas
items.body: The biggest and most explosive festival in the Mediterranean. From 1 to 19 March, Valencia becomes a museum of ephemeral art in the street: more than 350 falla commissions erect monuments several storeys high that burn on the night of the 19th. The mascletà thunders every midday in the Plaza del Ayuntamiento, the Flower Offering mobilises more than 100,000 falleros and the Nit del Foc lights up the sky in the early hours of the 18th to 19th. Declared an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2016.
facts: Last Sunday of February: the fallera mayor proclaims the start of Las Fallas from the Serranos Towers
From 1 to 19 March at 14:00 in the Plaza del Ayuntamiento
Night of 15 to 16 March: the monuments are raised in every neighbourhood
17 and 18 March: more than 100,000 falleros bring flowers to the Virgin of the Forsaken
Early hours of the 18th to 19th: the largest fireworks display in Spain
Night of 19 March: all the monuments burn in unison in every neighbourhood

items.title: Semana Santa Marinera (Seafarers’ Holy Week)
items.body: Spain’s most seafaring Holy Week is celebrated in the districts of El Cabanyal, Canyamelar and Cap de França, Valencia’s old fishing villages. Its processions are unique: the Cristo Yacente of the Semana Santa Marinera, the dressed figures and the intimate atmosphere of the fishing districts give it a different character from the processions of the interior. Declared an Asset of Cultural Interest.
facts: Procession of the Meeting (Procesión del Encuentro)
Palm Sunday: start of the events in the seafaring districts
Good Friday: the most moving procession, with the Cristo Yacente through the streets of El Cabanyal
Procession of Solitude (Procesión de la Soledad)
Holy Saturday: the Virgen de la Soledad walks through the districts in silence

items.title: Virgen de los Desamparados (Our Lady of the Forsaken) and Saint Vincent Ferrer
items.body: On the second Sunday of May, Valencia honours its patron with the grand procession of the Virgen de los Desamparados from the Basilica to the Cathedral. It is one of the most crowded and moving religious events in the city. A few days earlier, on Easter Monday, the feast of Saint Vincent Ferrer is celebrated with the popular Misteris de Sant Vicent: stagings of the miracles of the 14th-century Valencian Dominican saint on street altars.
facts: Easter Monday: nine stagings of the saint’s miracles in the streets of the centre
2nd Sunday of May: procession from the Basilica to the Cathedral before thousands of the faithful
The song to the Virgin sung by the crowd in the Plaza de la Virgen
2nd Sunday of May · Monday after Easter

items.title: Corpus Christi
items.body: Valencia’s Corpus Christi procession is one of the oldest and most important in Spain, with a cortege that has included unique elements since the 14th century: the rocas or processional floats – kept in the Corpus Museum – the Moma and the Misteris, allegorical figures representing the triumph of good over evil. It winds through the historic centre in an unrepeatable medieval spectacle.
facts: Medieval processional floats from the 14th century that parade through the historic centre
An allegorical figure representing good pursuing and defeating vice
The full cortege winds through the historic centre at dusk

items.kicker: Festive and popular · A month of celebration
items.title: Gran Fira de València
items.body: All through July Valencia celebrates its Gran Fira with an inexhaustible programme of concerts, bullfights, the Battle of Flowers, the band festival and nights of theatre and open-air shows in the Jardines de Viveros. The Battle of Flowers, in which floats throw petals at each other along the Paseo de la Alameda, is the most photogenic and joyful event of the fair.
facts: Last Sunday of July: decorated floats and flower petals on the Paseo de la Alameda
Free open-air shows in the Jardines de Viveros throughout July
Music festival with national and international artists at different venues
On some days in July there is also a mascletà in the Plaza del Ayuntamiento

items.title: 9 d’Octubre · Day of the Valencian Community
items.body: On 9 October 1238, King James I of Aragon entered Valencia with his troops and the city was reconquered from the Muslims. That day, declared the national holiday of the Valencian Community, is celebrated with a grand civic procession, the Processó Cívica, which winds through the historic centre with dignitaries, music bands and re-enactments of Valencian history. The events include the presentation of the Jaume I Awards.
facts: Civic parade through the historic centre with authorities, bands and Valencian groups
Gala of the most important awards of the Valencian Community
Events in the Plaza de la Virgen
Flower offering and institutional speeches in the heart of the city

items.title: Christmas in Valencia
items.body: The Valencian Christmas cycle has its own Mediterranean rhythm: the switching on of the lights at the end of November, the big Christmas tree in the Plaza del Ayuntamiento, the traditional market with nougat and crafts, the Toy Fair at Expojove, carol concerts at the Palau de la Música and the Three Kings Parade on 5 January, one of the oldest in Spain.
facts: End of November: more than 800,000 lights illuminate the historic centre
Plaza del Ayuntamiento: crafts, nougat and nativity figures all December
Spain’s biggest toy fair, a must for families
5 January: one of the oldest and most moving parades in Spain

blocks.title: What to know before experiencing Valencia’s festivals
items: All the main festivals are free and open to everyone
Las Fallas is the busiest event: book accommodation months in advance
During Las Fallas, public transport runs on extended special timetables
The Flower Offering (17–18 March) is a must: arrive early to see the parade
The mascletà starts exactly at 14:00 in the Plaza del Ayuntamiento
The Battle of Flowers in July: wear clothes you don’t mind getting covered in petals
